newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: FOCUS - ABB profit rises, dollar hides improvement.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - ABB profit rises, dollar hides improvement.

text.p: ABB Asea Brown Boveri AG on Thursday reported a smaller-than-expected rise in first half profits as the strong dollar hid a steady improvement in the electrical engineering group's operating earnings.
"Look at the operating performance and look at the currencies, this is a strong performance," ABB's chief executive Goran Lindahl told Reuters.
ABB's group net profit in the first six months of 1997 rose two percent to $567 million from last year, below the 4.5 percent rise that had been forecast by industry analysts.
After initial weakness on the results, ABB's shares in Switzerland recovered and were up 2.3 percent in mid-afternoon in a generally higher market.
ABB's first half operating earnings rose three percent to $1.09 billion, helped by all business segments, while revenue fell 2.6 percent to $15.2 billion on continued weak demand from Western Europe.
But Lindahl said the results were in line with what ABB had promised financial markets and some analysts had forgotten to take the strength of the dollar into account.

Although ABB is owned by Swedish and Swiss parent companies, the group reports in U.S. dollars. The strength of the dollar against European currencies tends to reduce its group results and inflate the results of its parent companies.
Expressed in local currencies, ABB's first half group net profit rose 12 percent and operating earnings 11 percent.
First half earnings per share of ABB's Swedish parent rose 12 percent to 2.26 crowns and earnings of its Swiss parent rose 22 percent to 45.40 Swiss francs.
But Lindahl was encouraged by the continued inflow of new orders to ABB and the growing backlog.
"In light of a better backlog, growing orders and that the business environment does not get worse, then it is encouraging for the future," Lindahl said.

Among the recent orders that ABB has received is work on Malaysia's Bakun hydroelectric dam. The total value of the project is $6.18 billion with ABB's share accounting for over $2.5 billion, the largest order it has ever received.

ABB and Bakun's main developer Ekran have recently been in new discussions over the project and Malaysia's prime minister has threatened to intervene and possibly cancel the contract if the dispute could not be resolved.
Lindahl, however, had no doubt about the project.
"I have no doubts the project will go ahead. These type of discussions are not unusual with these large, complex and visible-type project," Lindahl said.
New orders to ABB in the first half rose 14 percent to $20.0 billion -- pushing the order backlog up to $35.3 billion -- on strong growth in large projects and increased demand from emerging markets.
"This is a very good growth rate and show the efforts to penetrate markets, especially the emerging markets, is giving good rewards," Lindahl said.
ABB also confirmed its forecast for 1997 net profit to at least reach 1996's $1.233 billion, a forecast that Lindahl has described as setting a minimum for what profits could be.
Analysts on average forecast a 5.0 percent increase in ABB's 1997 net profit to $1.295 billion from 1996's $1.233 billion.
All ABB's segments contributed to the better operating peformance with the strongest regional growth coming from Poland and United Kingdom.
Profits from the U.S. also continued to improve and results from Latin America were substantiall higher than last year. Earnings from the Asian-Pacific region were unchanged.
ABB's worldwide workforce grew to 216,000 from 215,000, mainly due to new ventures and acquisitions.
